video_title: Lighthouse or Landgrab? How to Pick Your AI Sales Strategy
gist: a16z's Joe Schmidt and operating partner Andy (ex-Samsara, ex-Meraki sales leader, rendered 'Moroi' in the captions) lay out a 2x2 for enterprise AI go-to-market — buyer exposure versus whether proof travels — separating 'lighthouse' (win marquee regulated logos, sell with proof) from 'land grab' (displace existing budget in the mid-market, sell with math). Their bigger claim is that the 15-year PLG/land-and-expand era is over: AI has reopened the window to sell big platform software again, because buyers are willing to replace core systems rather than swap green buttons for blue ones.

insights.claim: a16z's framework maps enterprise AI go-to-market on two axes — the buyer's exposure (risk of being wrong, and whether the product is visible to their own end customers) and whether proof travels in that market — with high-exposure/proof-travels markets being lighthouse and low-exposure/proof-doesn't-travel markets being land grab.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Gives an investor a fast diligence question for any AI application company: which quadrant is it in, and does its sales spend match that quadrant?

insights.claim: The operative distinction between the two playbooks is what you sell with: lighthouse markets are sold with proof (reference logos), land grab markets are sold with math (a demonstrable cost or working-capital delta versus the incumbent solution).
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: If a company selling into an existing-budget market can't show the arithmetic, its sales problem is a product-value problem, not a brand problem.
insights.quote: the kind of distinction that we drew was between like proof on the the top right of the of the quadrant and math on the bottom left

insights.claim: Lighthouse markets are characterized by regulation, a constricted number of logos, and severe downside if the buyer picks wrong — up to regulatory trouble — which is why proof from an early marquee win transfers to the rest of the market.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: In regulated verticals, the first two or three logos are effectively the moat; watch for who lands them, because the rest of the category follows.

insights.claim: The practical test for which playbook you are in is behavioral, not analytical: if prospects will take the call, run a POC and buy, you are in a land grab; if they won't, you have to do deep forward-deployed lighthouse work to manufacture proof.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: A cheap, fast diagnostic that replaces months of GTM strategy debate — and a red flag when a company insists on lighthouse positioning while nobody will take meetings.

insights.claim: The strongest predictor of land grab suitability is an existing budget line and an incumbent (software or human) being replaced; a brand-new product requiring market education and internal budget creation is a lighthouse motion by default.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Budget-displacement companies should compound revenue faster and with cheaper sales; category-creation companies need to be underwritten on a longer, lumpier ramp.

insights.claim: The two playbooks are sequential rather than exclusive — nearly every large software company eventually runs both, typically starting land grab and verticalizing into lighthouse once it moves upmarket, as both Meraki and Samsara did.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Treat GTM strategy as stage-dependent; a company changing motions at scale is maturing, not flip-flopping.

themes.theme: Live examples in the AI portfolio

insights.claim: Harvey is presented as the archetypal lighthouse execution: it won a handful of critical law-firm accounts for a high-perceived-risk workload (automating junior-lawyer work), after which the proof travelled and made the purchase feel safe for other exposed buyers.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: The legal-AI category has already had its proof event, which raises the bar for later entrants — they must now displace, not evangelize.

insights.claim: The accounts-receivable AI company the partners call the prototypical land grab (rendered 'Stuart'/'STO' in the captions, founded by Tark and Ben) sells to the mid-market purely on math — collections effectiveness and working-capital improvement versus incumbent human teams plus legacy AR software — then expands into the full order-to-cash suite.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Back-office finance workflows with quantifiable working-capital ROI are the cleanest AI land grabs — the buyer needs no education, only a spreadsheet.

insights.claim: Pylon, an AI-native customer support company, is running the land grab motion by starting at modest ACVs and climbing the ACV ladder through pure displacement rather than category creation.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Climbing the ACV ladder from below is the observable signal that a displacement motion is working; flat ACV over several quarters means the engine has stalled.

insights.claim: Decagon is cited as best-in-class at evangelizing because it commits to specific benchmarks up front and then hits them in the stated period, which is how a vendor sells into a high-exposure market like customer support.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Pre-committed, measurable benchmarks are becoming the standard contract structure for agentic AI — a template competitors will have to match.

insights.claim: Further AI sells into insurance — an industry described as not a first adopter — by leading with governance-first, secure architecture plus forward-deployed teams, which is what makes the largest insurers comfortable buying.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: In laggard regulated verticals, governance architecture is the product wedge, not a compliance afterthought.

insights.claim: Applied Intuition (rendered 'applied to tuition' in the captions) is offered as a company that can stay lighthouse permanently, because the universe of autonomous-software buyers and car manufacturers is finite and each account is a huge ACV that must be handled with immense care.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Permanent-lighthouse businesses have concentrated revenue and long cycles — model them like defense contractors, not SaaS.

themes.theme: Regulatory catalysts and the AI 'why now'

insights.claim: Samsara's early traction came from the US ELD mandate phased in between 2016 and 2019, which forced the entire long-haul trucking industry to find budget for electronic logging devices at once and gave a new entrant a share of buyers actively shopping.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Compliance mandates are the cleanest demand catalyst in enterprise software — a forced budget event that lets challengers bypass incumbency; screen for pending mandates as a source of new entrants' revenue.

insights.claim: The current analogue to a regulatory mandate is CEO-level pressure: AI boards inside large enterprises are being told what to buy and by when, creating a temporary window of kinetic buying energy that the speakers expect to close.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Treat the current enterprise AI order flow as partly a mandate-like spending spike with a finite life — a reason to discount 2026 AI-application growth rates when extrapolating.

insights.claim: In 2017-18 Samsara deliberately targeted the mid-market rather than the largest trucking firms, because mid-market required less social proof and — critically — the short sales cycles produced far faster product feedback loops than large-account deployments.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Segment choice is a product-development decision as much as a revenue one: enterprise-first companies buy revenue at the cost of iteration speed.
insights.quote: The bigger the account, the longer these deployments, the longer the feedback loops.

insights.claim: Meraki won enterprise networking in 2009-10 against entrenched Cisco and HP not with features but with a distribution hack — free access points given to webinar attendees — betting that hands-on trial would demonstrate ease of use faster than any sales argument.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Liberal trial economics can be the cheapest customer acquisition channel when the product's advantage is experiential — a lens for judging today's generous AI free tiers.

themes.theme: POCs, pilots and the 'science project' trap

insights.claim: The central execution risk in AI enterprise sales today is that pilots become open-ended science projects, because the technology improves daily so every 'can it also do X' request can plausibly be answered yes.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Watch pilot-to-production conversion and pilot duration as the leading indicator of AI application revenue quality — capability velocity actively works against closing.
insights.quote: the real dangers today is these things turn into like science projects

insights.claim: The prescribed discipline is two non-negotiables in every trial: a hard end date (30/45/60 days) and success criteria defined up front, with both sides agreeing in advance that meeting them triggers the purchase.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence question for any AI vendor: what fraction of pilots have a contractual end date and pre-agreed success criteria?

insights.claim: AI vendors face a distinctive scoping hazard: they can be held responsible both for whether the product works and for whether the customer deploys and uses it correctly, which are separate problems that pilots conflate.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Outcome-based AI contracts silently transfer customer-execution risk onto the vendor — a margin risk that doesn't show up until renewal cohorts do.

themes.theme: The end of the PLG cycle — big software is sellable again

insights.claim: The 2010-2024 dominance of PLG and land-and-expand was a function of where the industry sat in the adoption cycle: the big platform categories (CRM, HR, ITSM, security) were founded 2000-2010, so new entrants could only wedge in with a narrow product and expand.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: Reframes PLG as a cycle artifact rather than a permanent best practice — the GTM benchmarks investors internalized in the 2010s may not be the right comps for 2026 AI companies.

insights.claim: Cloud-to-cloud replacement failed because the switch offered no fundamental change, but AI is different in kind — buyers are willing to reconsider even CRM, HR and ITSM because the work itself moves to agents rather than being a skeuomorphic one-to-one replacement.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: The direct implication is incumbent-platform displacement risk that cloud-era logic said was impossible — the bear case for entrenched application software multiples.
insights.quote: I don't care if the button is green or blue. I don't care if there's like one little feature difference. I'm not going to switch.

insights.claim: The stated conclusion is that there is a live window to sell large platform software again, and founders should be studying pre-PLG enterprise playbooks from 15+ years ago rather than the last cycle's motions.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z)
insights.so_what: If correct, expect AI application companies to build expensive direct enterprise sales forces — higher S&M intensity than the PLG comps investors are used to underwriting.
insights.quote: There's a moment right now to go sell big software again.

insights.claim: Every technology transition leaves buyers more educated than the last, so today's enterprise buyer arrives already knowing what they want — shifting the vendor's job from education to differentiation.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Shorter education cycles should compress time-to-close and favor vendors with sharp comparative positioning over those with the best evangelism content.

insights.claim: The recommended ACV discipline is binary: check that the deal size clears your unit-economics hurdle, then stop optimizing and take as many of those deals as possible — ACV rises on its own as the company stacks wins and moves upmarket.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: A counter to the common instinct to chase deal size early — repeatability, not deal size, is what compounds.
insights.quote: if you can build a go to market engine just theoretically that could live off of 15k ACV deals, yeah, fantastic. Like don't take 8K ACV deals, but go get as many 15K AC deals as you can.

insights.claim: Seller profiles should be matched to the playbook: lighthouse motions need seasoned enterprise reps who know procurement cycles in target accounts, while land grab motions should hire earlier-career reps for attitude and aptitude and maximize coverage.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: A mismatch between rep seniority and motion is a diagnosable cause of stalled ARR growth in diligence conversations.

insights.claim: Verticalizing into a new segment (public sector, school districts, cities) requires a separate team because the sales cycle, decision makers and procurement process differ fundamentally from mid-market selling.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Expect a sales-productivity dip whenever a company announces a public-sector push with the existing team — the motion doesn't transfer.

insights.claim: Companies where only 40-50% of reps hit quota are doing themselves a disservice at the early stage — either quotas are too high or the hiring profile is wrong — because early sales orgs run on momentum and attract talent by being winnable.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Quota attainment below ~60% early is a talent-retention risk, not evidence of ambition; cost of sales in the land-grab phase is the wrong thing to optimize.

insights.claim: The most commonly under-hired early role is sales operations — even one person owning territory alignment, name lists, commission disputes and the sales constitution — because unresolved, those become speed bumps at scale.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: A cheap operational tell in diligence: does a company at scale-up stage have dedicated sales ops, or is the sales leader still doing territories?

insights.claim: The biggest early-stage founder mistake identified is over-deliberating GTM strategy: spend roughly 1% of time choosing the playbook and 99% executing, because there are no bonus multipliers for hard-earned revenue from a marquee logo.
insights.speaker: Andy (a16z operating partner, ex-Samsara/Meraki)
insights.so_what: Logo prestige is not valued at a premium in revenue quality — a caution against paying up for companies whose story is marquee customers rather than repeatable volume.
insights.quote: There's no bonus points for hard-earned revenue.
